story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So now they overdub, as they call it. And that used to be against the rules. You know, now they -- how many tracks do they call it on a tape machine, like the average home tape machine is about two tracks.

There's one for each instrument in the band. You don't have to follow dynamics. If they don't like what you did the guy will sit in the control booth -- it's like that story about Toscanini, years before tape, listening to this recording of Mozart. In the booth he turns to the guy in the control room and said, "That's not Mozart, that's not me, that's you." He said, "Go home, set all the dials in the middle and sit on your hands. We make the dynamics, not you." But those days are gone. And now it's a man in the booth makes all the dynamics. He's the authority now.
That's right. What do they call it, after the workers leave they have a session where they balance.
Well now -- what is this digital recording they've got now?
Oh, that's right to the record. And they can work it (inaudible).
Oh, like they used to do? I thought it was something like they put it all down into numbers.
But you know, if you didn't like it in one number you put it in another number, get a different note.
